inicio.text:
Astra is a generic tabletop RPG system, designed to serve different settings, genres and play styles. Characters are built freely, without classes or levels, and conflicts can be resolved narratively or tactically, on a map.
The rules are organized into a core, shared by every table, on top of which modules can be built to add rules for specific needs, such as magic or vehicles. Each setting chooses the modules it uses and can adjust parts of the core, such as Creature Types and available equipment, without having to rewrite it.
At the heart of Astra is the resolution of the Storyteller family: d10 Dice Pools, superficial and aggravated damage, Willpower, Ambition, Desire and Convictions. On top of it, play is organized in the format of Pathfinder 2e and Dungeons & Dragons: Turns with an Action and Movement, combat on a square grid, Conditions, weapon properties and Competencies that advance by Levels.
The system is tightly integrated with Foundry Virtual Tabletop, which works as its main digital implementation. The goal, however, is not to limit Astra to the virtual table: its rules are designed so they can be used both at in-person tables and on other platforms.
How to play
A game of Astra brings together a Narrator and a group of players. Each player controls a character, called a player character. The Narrator describes the world and the situations, plays every other character, called NPCs, and applies the rules.
When a character attempts something whose outcome is uncertain, the player makes a test: they roll ten-sided dice and count the Successes (see Basic Mechanics).
Start here
To get to know the system, this is the recommended reading order:
Basic Mechanics — understand how tests are built and resolved.
Characters — learn the characters' capabilities and resources.
Character Creation — build a complete character.
Scenes and Conflicts — see how scenes, turns and confrontations work.
System rules
The core is organized into ten main areas, in the order in which they depend on each other:
Basic Mechanics — resolving tests and results.
Characters — the characters' capabilities, resources, motivations and traits.
Scenes and Conflicts — structure of tactical scenes, turns and confrontation actions.
Moving — getting around and actions related to movement.
Equipment — load, common items, Consumables, weapons, armor, shields and switching items.
Resistance and Vulnerability — how characters and creatures react to damage types.
Conditions — states that affect characters during a scene.
Competencies — sets of Capabilities that change what the character can do.
Capabilities — single list of Competency Capabilities and NPC Capabilities, with the rules for their use by NPCs.
Creatures — NPC sheet, creating NPCs, bestiary and creature types.
All rules on this page belong to the core. Modules, when they exist, live in their own folders.
Character creation
To build a character, follow the steps in Character Creation.

regras/mecanica-basica/reserva-de-dados.title: Dice Pool
regras/mecanica-basica/reserva-de-dados.summary: The Dice Pool is the number of dice used to resolve an action whose outcome is uncertain. The larger the Pool, the better the character's chances of a good result.
regras/mecanica-basica/reserva-de-dados.text:
The Dice Pool is the number of dice used to resolve an action whose outcome is uncertain. The larger the Pool, the better the character's chances of a good result.
Dice Used
Astra uses ten-sided dice, written with the abbreviation d10. Each point of the Dice Pool is one d10 rolled: a Pool of 5 dice means rolling 5d10.
Building a Dice Pool
When a character tries something that requires a test, the rule in use or the Narrator determines which Skill applies. The Pool is the Skill plus its linked Attribute, listed in Skills.
Attribute + Skill = Dice Pool
For example, a character with Agility 3 and Stealth 2 trying to slip quietly through a guarded area rolls Agility + Stealth, a Pool of 5 dice.
When no Skill applies to the action, the Pool is formed by the Attribute alone. For example, resisting a poison might use only Vigor.
Every Dice Pool has at least one Attribute. The second part, when there is one, is a Skill or another Attribute, never the same Attribute twice.
The linked Attribute only changes when a rule expressly says so (see Attribute Replacements).
Successes
Roll all the dice in the Pool. Each die showing 6 or more is a Success.
Result Effect 
1 - 5 No Success 
6 - 9 1 Success 
10 1 Success (a pair of 10s grants 1 extra Success) 
A result of 1 has no special effect: it simply does not count as a Success.
Pairs of 10s
When two dice show 10 on the same roll, they form a pair of 10s. Each pair grants 1 extra Success, on top of the 2 Successes the dice already produced.
10 + 10 = 3 Successes
Each pair of 10s is counted separately. An unpaired 10 counts normally as 1 Success. For example, the results 10, 10, 10, 7, 3 produce 5 Successes: the pair of 10s produces 3, the third 10 produces 1 and the 7 produces 1 more.
Difficulty
A test's Difficulty is the number of Successes needed for the action to succeed. The test succeeds when the number of Successes is equal to or greater than the Difficulty. Otherwise, the result is a Failure.
Difficulty Scale
The table below is a suggested calibration, not a firm rule. The Narrator can adjust it to the situation.
Difficulty Description 
1 Routine: almost always works 
2 Basic: standard for most tests 
3 Challenging: takes a little effort 
4 Hard: needs a good Pool 
5 Very hard: few even try 
6+ Feat: reserved for extraordinary deeds 
An average character (Attribute 2 + Skill 2, a Pool of 4 dice) has good odds at Difficulty 2. Use it as a starting point.
Extra Successes
Matching the Difficulty already guarantees success. Each Success above the Difficulty, however, deserves special treatment: the action can be finished faster, more elegantly or more discreetly, reveal extra information or open new opportunities. The bigger the surplus, the more impressive the result. It is up to the Narrator to reward the surplus narratively.
Example: with a Pool of 5 dice, a character gets 2, 6, 10, 10, 4. The 6 produces 1 Success and the pair of 10s produces 3, for a total of 4 Successes. Against Difficulty 4 or less, the action succeeds; against Difficulty 5 or more, it is a Failure.
Opposed Tests
In an opposed test, two characters roll their Dice Pools and whoever gets more Successes wins. For example, the Stealth of someone hiding against the Perception of someone searching.
On a tie, the current situation stands: whoever is trying to change something fails. Specific rules, such as Confront, can set a different result for a tie.
Penalties
Dice penalties, such as those from Prone, Debilitated, Grappled and Overload, add up. A character who is Prone and Debilitated, for example, suffers -4 dice.
Some penalties only affect rolls of one category, Physical or Spiritual (see Attributes). A roll's category is determined by the Attribute actually used, including after a replacement. When the Pool combines two Attributes of different categories, the penalties of both categories apply, and they also add up.
Minimum Pool
Penalties never reduce a Dice Pool below 1 die. A heavily penalized character still rolls 1 die.
The exception is a rule stating that the action cannot be taken when the Pool falls below 1 die, such as an Attack beyond Range in Confront.
Attribute Replacements
A Skill only uses another Attribute when an Action, equipment, Capability or other rule expressly says so. Describing the same action in a different way does not, by itself, change the linked Attribute.
When a Pool uses a Skill, determine its Attribute in this order:
the Skill sets its linked Attribute;
an Action, equipment or another rule can replace that Attribute;
a Capability can set another Attribute and always takes precedence over the previous steps.
For example, Fighting is linked to Agility. A melee Attack normally uses Agility + Fighting. If the weapon has a property that sets Strength, the Attack uses Strength + Fighting. If a Capability sets Cunning as the Attribute of that Attack, the final Pool is Cunning + Fighting.
A replacement follows these principles:
it swaps one Attribute for another: only the final Attribute is added to the Skill;
its effect is limited to the Skill, Action, Pool or formula it names;
replacements do not chain to add several Attributes;
when more than one optional replacement is available, the character picks only one.
The narrative approach can still change the applicable Skill, the Difficulty, the effects of a win or failure and any circumstantial bonuses or penalties. It just does not freely replace a Skill's Attribute.
Help
Other characters can help whoever is making a test. Helpers do not roll dice. Help adds +1 die to the Dice Pool of whoever makes the test.
There is no limit on helpers, but the bonus does not stack: the test gets at most +1 die of help, no matter how many characters help.
In a Tactical Scene, a helper must be adjacent to whoever makes the test and uses their Action. Outside one, it is enough that the helper can actually take part in the task, at the Narrator's discretion.
Example: a character with Research 2 looks for information in a library with two allies helping. Their Pool gets +1 die.

regras/personagens/personagens.text:
This section gathers the elements that define a character's capabilities, resources, motivations and particularities.
Character creation
Character Creation — how to build a character from scratch.
Attributes and Skills
Attributes — fundamental physical and spiritual abilities.
Skills — knowledge and abilities the character has developed.
Nature
Size — physical build, space taken up on the map and who can move whom.
Creature Types — classification of the character's or creature's nature.
Resources
Health — physical condition, damage and recovery.
Willpower — determination and mental and emotional endurance.
Long Rest — recovery of superficial Health and Willpower damage.
Identity and customization
Ambition and Desire — long-term and short-term goals.
Convictions and Pillars — principles the character upholds and what sustains them.
Competencies — sets of Capabilities that change what the character can do.
Advancement
Advancement — earning and spending XP during the campaign.
Connections
These traits feed the Dice Pool and are used during Scenes and Conflicts.

regras/personagens/atributos.title: Attributes
regras/personagens/atributos.summary: Attributes represent a character's fundamental abilities. They describe their physical and spiritual aptitudes and are part of most Dice Pools used during play. Whenever an action calls for a test, a Skill is usually…
regras/personagens/atributos.text:
Attributes represent a character's fundamental abilities. They describe their physical and spiritual aptitudes and are part of most Dice Pools used during play.
Whenever an action calls for a test, a Skill is usually combined with its linked Attribute to form the Dice Pool.
For example, lifting a heavy object might call for Strength, while quickly noticing something out of the ordinary might involve Cunning.
Scale
A character's Attributes range from 1 to 5:
Value Meaning 
1 Weak 
2 Average, the norm for an ordinary adult 
3 Notable 
4 Exceptional 
5 Human peak 
Creatures that are not human can have Attributes above 5; characters are limited to 5.
Categories
Each Attribute belongs to a category: Physical or Spiritual.
Category Attributes 
Physical Strength, Agility, Vigor 
Spiritual Charisma, Determination, Cunning 
Some penalties only affect rolls of one category, such as those of Debilitated, Overload and full Willpower. See how they apply in Penalties.
Linked Attributes and replacements
Each Skill has a linked Attribute, which forms its default Pool. It only changes when a rule expressly says so (see Attribute Replacements).
Capabilities can also replace Attributes in fixed formulas, such as Health, Willpower, Load or Initiative. That replacement affects only the given formula and does not change the other roles of the Attributes involved.
List of Attributes
Strength
Represents the character's physical power.
It is used to lift, carry, push, break or exert force against something. It is linked to Athletics and Throwing, takes part in physical Maneuvers, sets Load and replaces Agility on Attacks made with Heavy weapons.
Agility
Represents coordination, reflexes and bodily precision.
It is used in actions that depend on quick movements, balance, motor control or physical precision. It is the default Attribute for melee and shooting-weapon Attacks, and is linked to Acrobatics, Shooting, Riding, Driving, Stealth, Fighting, Piloting and Sleight of Hand.
Vigor
Represents physical endurance, toughness and the ability to withstand effort.
It is used to resist fatigue, harsh conditions and other situations that put the body to the test. It also sets the default number of boxes on the Health track.
Charisma
Represents presence, personal magnetism and the ability to influence other people.
It is used when the character tries to inspire, please, impress, persuade, deceive or lead someone in a given direction. It is linked to Animal Empathy, Intimidation, Deception, Performance and Persuasion.
Determination
Represents focus, discipline, emotional stability and mental strength.
It is used to keep concentration, stay calm, persist in the face of hardship and resist provocations, pressures and influences that try to steer the character away from their goals. It also sets the default number of boxes on the Willpower track and, together with Cunning, forms the Initiative Pool.
Cunning
Represents knowledge, reasoning, quick thinking and perception.
It is used to understand problems, research, remember information, notice the surroundings, improvise and find solutions — including under time pressure. It is linked to General Knowledge, Repair, Healing, Scholarship, Navigation, Occultism, Perception, Research and Survival. It also takes part in Initiative and limits the normal stacks of Aiming.

regras/personagens/pericias.title: Skills
regras/personagens/pericias.summary: Skills represent trained abilities and areas of knowledge a character has developed through practice, study or experience. They do not describe innate talent, but what the character has learned to do. Each Skill has a…
regras/personagens/pericias.text:
Skills represent trained abilities and areas of knowledge a character has developed through practice, study or experience. They do not describe innate talent, but what the character has learned to do.
Each Skill has a linked Attribute, normally used to form its Dice Pool.
Linked Attribute + Skill = Dice Pool
The description of the action determines which Skill applies. The linked Attribute only changes when a rule expressly says so (see Attribute Replacements).
Scale
Skills range from 0 to 5:
Value Meaning 
0 Untrained 
1 Beginner 
2 Competent 
3 Expert 
4 Master 
5 Leading authority 
A Skill at 0 adds no dice: the Pool is formed by the Attribute alone.
List of Skills
Skill Linked Attribute Description 
Acrobatics Agility Dodging, keeping balance, breaking falls and performing precise body movements. 
Throwing Strength Hurling weapons and objects directly with the body, such as knives, spears, stones and grenades. 
Shooting Agility Firing projectile weapons, such as bows, crossbows and firearms. 
Athletics Strength Running, jumping, climbing, swimming and other feats of physical power. 
Riding Agility Mounting, steering and keeping control of ridden animals. 
General Knowledge Cunning Common knowledge of the world and of one's own culture: customs, places, laws, figures and news. 
Repair Cunning Repairing, assembling and taking apart mechanisms, equipment and structures. 
Healing Cunning Treating wounds, illnesses and other physical conditions. 
Driving Agility Driving motorized land vehicles. 
Animal Empathy Charisma Calming, training, understanding and bonding with animals. 
Scholarship Cunning Academic knowledge: history, sciences, literate culture and the like. 
Stealth Agility Moving unnoticed, hiding and acting silently. 
Intimidation Charisma Coercing someone through threats, pressure or posture. 
Fighting Agility Melee combat, unarmed or with weapons. 
Deception Charisma Deceiving, bluffing and keeping up falsehoods. 
Navigation Cunning Finding the way and plotting routes over land, sea or air. 
Occultism Cunning Supernatural knowledge, rituals and mysteries. 
Perception Cunning Noticing details, sounds, movements and presences nearby. 
Performance Charisma Entertaining, acting, singing, dancing or performing before an audience. 
Persuasion Charisma Convincing someone through arguments, appeal or smooth talk. 
Research Cunning Investigating, seeking information and analyzing clues and documents. 
Piloting Agility Flying aircraft and operating other complex vehicles. 
Sleight of Hand Agility Performing quick feats with the hands: pickpocketing, hiding objects and doing tricks. 
Survival Cunning Getting by in hostile environments: hunting, tracking, building shelter and finding resources. 
Languages
Every character knows the common language of their region. Each Level in Scholarship grants one additional language, chosen by the player and recorded on the character sheet.
Specific Knowledge
General Knowledge covers the character's average knowledge of any subject. For in-depth mastery of a topic, the character acquires a Specific Knowledge: a Skill with a free subject, such as Poisons, Heraldry or Northern Folklore, always linked to Cunning.
Each Specific Knowledge is a separate Skill, with its own Level, and follows the same distribution and cost rules as the other Skills.
On tests about its subject, the character can use the Specific Knowledge instead of General Knowledge, Scholarship or Occultism. The Narrator can also decide that certain information, such as rare details and trade secrets, is only within reach of someone with the matching Specific Knowledge.
Skills by Setting
This list represents Astra's default core, but each setting is free to add, remove or replace Skills to fit the world and the campaign's premise.
A medieval setting would have no Driving or Piloting, since those vehicles do not exist. In exchange, it could include its own Skills, such as Etiquette or Command.
A science fiction setting would keep Piloting and could add Skills such as Hacking or Engineering.
regras/personagens/pericias.html:
Skills represent trained abilities and areas of knowledge a character has developed through practice, study or experience. They do not describe innate talent, but what the character has learned to do.

Each Skill has a linked Attribute, normally used to form its Dice Pool.

Linked Attribute + Skill = Dice Pool

The description of the action determines which Skill applies. The linked Attribute only changes when a rule expressly says so (see Attribute Replacements).

Scale

Skills range from 0 to 5:

ValueMeaning
0Untrained
1Beginner
2Competent
3Expert
4Master
5Leading authority

A Skill at 0 adds no dice: the Pool is formed by the Attribute alone.

List of Skills

SkillLinked AttributeDescription
AcrobaticsAgilityDodging, keeping balance, breaking falls and performing precise body movements.
ThrowingStrengthHurling weapons and objects directly with the body, such as knives, spears, stones and grenades.
ShootingAgilityFiring projectile weapons, such as bows, crossbows and firearms.
AthleticsStrengthRunning, jumping, climbing, swimming and other feats of physical power.
RidingAgilityMounting, steering and keeping control of ridden animals.
General KnowledgeCunningCommon knowledge of the world and of one's own culture: customs, places, laws, figures and news.
RepairCunningRepairing, assembling and taking apart mechanisms, equipment and structures.
HealingCunningTreating wounds, illnesses and other physical conditions.
DrivingAgilityDriving motorized land vehicles.
Animal EmpathyCharismaCalming, training, understanding and bonding with animals.
ScholarshipCunningAcademic knowledge: history, sciences, literate culture and the like.
StealthAgilityMoving unnoticed, hiding and acting silently.
IntimidationCharismaCoercing someone through threats, pressure or posture.
FightingAgilityMelee combat, unarmed or with weapons.
DeceptionCharismaDeceiving, bluffing and keeping up falsehoods.
NavigationCunningFinding the way and plotting routes over land, sea or air.
OccultismCunningSupernatural knowledge, rituals and mysteries.
PerceptionCunningNoticing details, sounds, movements and presences nearby.
PerformanceCharismaEntertaining, acting, singing, dancing or performing before an audience.
PersuasionCharismaConvincing someone through arguments, appeal or smooth talk.
ResearchCunningInvestigating, seeking information and analyzing clues and documents.
PilotingAgilityFlying aircraft and operating other complex vehicles.
Sleight of HandAgilityPerforming quick feats with the hands: pickpocketing, hiding objects and doing tricks.
SurvivalCunningGetting by in hostile environments: hunting, tracking, building shelter and finding resources.

Languages

Every character knows the common language of their region. Each Level in Scholarship grants one additional language, chosen by the player and recorded on the character sheet.

Specific Knowledge

General Knowledge covers the character's average knowledge of any subject. For in-depth mastery of a topic, the character acquires a Specific Knowledge: a Skill with a free subject, such as Poisons, Heraldry or Northern Folklore, always linked to Cunning.

Each Specific Knowledge is a separate Skill, with its own Level, and follows the same distribution and cost rules as the other Skills.

On tests about its subject, the character can use the Specific Knowledge instead of General Knowledge, Scholarship or Occultism. The Narrator can also decide that certain information, such as rare details and trade secrets, is only within reach of someone with the matching Specific Knowledge.

  • A medieval setting would have no Driving or Piloting, since those vehicles do not exist. In exchange, it could include its own Skills, such as Etiquette or Command.
  • A science fiction setting would keep Piloting and could add Skills such as Hacking or Engineering.

regras/personagens/tamanho.title: Size
regras/personagens/tamanho.summary: Size gives the physical build of a character or creature and how much space they take up on the map during a Tactical Scene. Every character has a Size. The default is Medium. Size Space taken up. Tiny shares a square…
regras/personagens/tamanho.text:
Size gives the physical build of a character or creature and how much space they take up on the map during a Tactical Scene.
Every character has a Size. The default is Medium.
Size Space taken up 
Tiny shares a square 
Small 1 × 1 square 
Medium 1 × 1 square 
Large 2 × 2 squares 
Huge 3 × 3 squares 
Colossal 4 × 4 squares 
A creature that takes up more than one square is considered adjacent to everything next to any of the squares it occupies, including diagonally.
A Tiny creature can occupy the same square as another creature and can be moved through by anyone.
Size Limit
A creature can only Grapple, Trip or move against their will a target at most one category larger than itself.
The limit applies to the Grapple, Trip and Reposition Maneuvers, to dragging a Grappled target and to any other rule that moves a character against their will. Disarm has no Size limit.
Size in the Attack
Attacking a much larger target is easier, and attacking a much smaller target is harder. Count the difference in categories between the attacker and the target:
Target Attack 
2 categories larger +2 dice 
3 or more categories larger +4 dice 
2 or more categories smaller -2 dice 
One category of difference changes nothing. The rule works both ways: a cat attacking a dragon gets +4 dice, and the dragon attacking the cat gets -2.
Settings and modules can define additional rules for Size.

regras/personagens/vida.title: Health
regras/personagens/vida.summary: Health represents a character's physical condition and their ability to keep acting after being wounded. Whenever a character takes damage, that damage is recorded on their Health track. As wounds pile up, their…
regras/personagens/vida.text:
Health represents a character's physical condition and their ability to keep acting after being wounded.
Whenever a character takes damage, that damage is recorded on their Health track. As wounds pile up, their condition worsens until they can no longer carry on as usual.
Health does not represent only visible wounds. It can also represent physical exhaustion, trauma, burns, bruises and other consequences that can compromise the character's body.
Health Track
Each character has a limited number of boxes on their Health track:
3 + Vigor boxes
Vigor is the Health Attribute by default. Settings, Capabilities and other rules can adjust this value or replace the Attribute used in the formula.
When a Capability replaces Vigor, the number of boxes is recalculated immediately from the new Attribute. The replacement only affects the size of the track: recovery, Vigor tests and other rules are not changed, unless the Capability itself says otherwise.
When they take damage, the player marks a number of boxes equal to the damage taken. Keep aggravated damage on the left of the track and superficial damage on the right.
Damage Severity
Astra uses two damage severities: superficial and aggravated. The difference between them represents how serious the wound is and what it takes to recover from it.
By default, all damage is aggravated. The exception is damage that its own source marks as superficial, such as Unarmed attacks and Nonlethal weapons. The Narrator can also decide that other sources deal superficial damage when the situation calls for it.
Armor and Resistances can convert aggravated damage into superficial damage at the moment it is taken.
The Damage Type, the nature of the wound (slashing, bludgeoning, piercing, fire, cold, electric and so on), is separate from severity. It is set by the source of the damage, such as Weapons.
Superficial Damage
Superficial damage represents lesser wounds, physical wear and traumas a character can recover from with relative ease: unarmed blows, light impacts and wounds that do not put their body at immediate risk.
It is recorded on the Health track as a / mark.
Aggravated Damage
Aggravated damage represents serious and potentially incapacitating wounds: deep cuts and stabs, severe burns, lethal electricity and other especially dangerous forms of damage.
It is recorded on the Health track as an X.
Full Health Track
When the Health track is full, with any combination of superficial and aggravated damage, the character becomes Debilitated.
With the track full, each point of additional damage, superficial or aggravated, converts 1 box of superficial damage into aggravated.
When the whole track is filled with aggravated damage, the character becomes Incapacitated. The fate of an Incapacitated character who keeps taking damage is up to the Narrator.
Recovery
Wounds do not vanish as soon as a conflict ends. Recovery depends on the severity of the damage taken.
Superficial damage heals with time. When completing a Long Rest, the character recovers an amount of superficial damage equal to their Vigor.
Aggravated damage does not recover with time. It is only converted into superficial damage through Treatment. After that, it heals normally.
Treatment
Outside a Tactical Scene, a character with healing supplies, such as a Healing Kit, can treat themselves or another character. Without supplies, treatment is not possible.
Whoever treats rolls Cunning + Healing. Each Success converts 1 point of aggravated damage into superficial. With no Successes, nothing is converted.
Each character receives at most one Treatment per day. An Incapacitated character cannot treat themselves.
Proper Facilities
In a hospital or an equivalent place, Treatment needs no healing supplies, gets +2 dice and converts at least 3 points of aggravated damage. If no one in the group can treat, the facility's staff guarantees that minimum.

regras/personagens/vontade.title: Willpower
regras/personagens/vontade.summary: Willpower is a resource: the character spends it to push past their own limits. While Health represents the character's physical condition, the damage built up on the Willpower track represents the state of their…
regras/personagens/vontade.text:
Willpower is a resource: the character spends it to push past their own limits. While Health represents the character's physical condition, the damage built up on the Willpower track represents the state of their psyche: the strain of that effort and the marks left by their Convictions.
Willpower Track
Each character has a limited number of boxes on their Willpower track:
3 + Determination boxes
Determination is the Willpower Attribute by default. Settings, Capabilities and other rules can adjust this value or replace the Attribute used in the formula.
When a Capability replaces Determination, the number of boxes is immediately recalculated from the new Attribute. The replacement affects only the size of the track: Determination tests, Initiative and other rules are not changed, unless the Capability itself says otherwise.
Willpower damage is marked as on the Health track: aggravated damage stays on the left of the track and superficial damage on the right.
Damage Severity
Like Health, Willpower takes superficial and aggravated damage.
By default, all Willpower damage is superficial. It is aggravated only when the source says so, such as Conviction Fractures and Break Limit.
Willpower damage does not count as taking damage: when a rule speaks of taking damage without mentioning Willpower, it refers to Health.
Superficial damage represents stress, frustration, momentary fear and other strain the character recovers from relatively quickly.
Aggravated damage represents trauma and deep marks on the character's state of mind, which can stay with them for a long time. Each Fracture a Conviction receives deals 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage (see Convictions and Pillars).
Full Willpower
When the Willpower track is full, with any mix of superficial and aggravated damage, the character suffers -2 dice on rolls that use a Spiritual Attribute.
With the track full, each point of extra damage, superficial or aggravated, converts 1 box of superficial damage into aggravated, as on the Health track.
When the whole track is filled with aggravated damage, the -2 dice penalty applies to every roll, in place of the Spiritual penalty, and the character suffers a consequence that depends on the origin and nature of the trauma. It lasts until at least 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage becomes superficial.
This consequence does not necessarily mean unconsciousness or total loss of control. The Narrator sets it according to the circumstances of the scene, for example:
freezing in the face of the situation;
emotional collapse;
flight;
giving up;
momentary loss of control;
inability to keep facing a given threat.
Using Willpower
When using Willpower, the character takes 1 point of superficial Willpower damage and chooses one of the effects below. Some Capabilities granted by Competencies also require using Willpower.
With a full Willpower track, any use of Willpower is paid by Breaking Limit.
Once per session, in total, a Conviction lets them Reroll Dice or Ignore Physical Penalties without taking the superficial damage, even with a full track. This benefit does not pay the Willpower costs of Capabilities (see Convictions and Pillars).
Reroll Dice
After making a test, the character can take 1 point of superficial Willpower damage to reroll up to 3 dice of their Dice Pool. The player chooses which dice are rerolled and must use the new results.
It is possible to reroll more than once on the same test, taking 1 point of superficial Willpower damage each time.
On an opposed roll, whoever started the action (for example, the attacker in a Confront) decides first whether to reroll. Then the other participant decides.
Ignore Physical Penalties
The character can take 1 point of superficial Willpower damage to ignore, on the roll where Willpower is used, the dice penalties caused by their physical condition, such as those of Debilitated, Poisoned, Prone, Grappled and Overload.
For example, a Debilitated character normally suffers -2 dice on rolls that use a Physical Attribute. By using Willpower, they can ignore that penalty on that roll.
Break Limit
When the Willpower track is full and still has superficial damage on it, the character can keep using Willpower by Breaking Limit. This applies to any use of Willpower, including the Willpower costs of Capabilities.
Each point of Willpower damage the use would deal converts 1 point of superficial Willpower damage into aggravated damage, as in Full Willpower.
With the track entirely filled with aggravated damage, it is not possible to Break Limit.
Recovery
Willpower damage does not disappear at the end of conflicts. Recovery depends on the severity of the damage taken.
Superficial damage: on completing a Long Rest, the character recovers all superficial Willpower damage. Acting to fulfill their Desire also recovers superficial damage (see Ambition and Desire).
Aggravated damage: does not recover with time. It becomes superficial when the character actively works toward their Ambition, when the character turns to a Pillar (1 point, once per session), when a Conviction Fracture is repaired (1 point) or when a broken Conviction is restored (up to 2 points) (see Convictions and Pillars).

regras/personagens/descanso-prolongado.title: Long Rest
regras/personagens/descanso-prolongado.summary: A Long Rest represents several continuous hours of rest, usually a night's sleep, in conditions that let the character rest and recover. On completing a Long Rest, the character: recovers an amount of superficial Health…
regras/personagens/descanso-prolongado.text:
A Long Rest represents several continuous hours of rest, usually a night's sleep, in conditions that let the character rest and recover.
On completing a Long Rest, the character:
recovers an amount of superficial Health damage equal to their Vigor;
recovers all superficial Willpower damage.
A Long Rest neither recovers nor converts aggravated Health or Willpower damage.
If the rest is interrupted by a conflict or other significant effort, it is not completed and must be started over. Brief interruptions, such as waking up for a watch shift, do not prevent the rest.
A character can only get the benefits of a Long Rest once per day.
regras/personagens/descanso-prolongado.html:
A Long Rest represents several continuous hours of rest, usually a night's sleep, in conditions that let the character rest and recover.

On completing a Long Rest, the character:

  • recovers an amount of superficial Health damage equal to their Vigor;
  • recovers all superficial Willpower damage.

A Long Rest neither recovers nor converts aggravated Health or Willpower damage.

If the rest is interrupted by a conflict or other significant effort, it is not completed and must be started over. Brief interruptions, such as waking up for a watch shift, do not prevent the rest.

A character can only get the benefits of a Long Rest once per day.

regras/personagens/ambicao-e-desejo.title: Ambition and Desire
regras/personagens/ambicao-e-desejo.summary: Characters are defined not only by their abilities, but also by what they want to achieve. Ambition and Desire represent the goals that guide a character's decisions, at different scales: Ambition is a long-term goal…

headings.title: Ambition and Desire in the Story

regras/personagens/ambicao-e-desejo.html:
Characters are defined not only by their abilities, but also by what they want to achieve. Ambition and Desire represent the goals that guide a character's decisions, at different scales: Ambition is a long-term goal, and Desire is something they want to achieve more immediately.

Each character has 1 Ambition and 1 Desire at a time.

Ambition

Ambition represents an important, lasting goal. It usually cannot be completed in a single scene or session and requires several steps, decisions or events.

Examples of Ambitions:

  • gaining a position of influence;
  • finding a missing person;
  • destroying a rival organization;
  • discovering the origin of a mysterious phenomenon;
  • recovering a lost object;
  • protecting a community;
  • becoming known as the best in a given field.

The Ambition should be broad enough to stay relevant for a significant part of the story and specific enough that it is possible to recognize when the character works toward it.

Progressing in an Ambition

At the end of a session in which the character actively worked toward their Ambition, 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage becomes superficial damage. Discovering important information, removing an obstacle, winning over an ally or completing a necessary step are examples of active work.

Changing the Ambition

The Ambition can be changed at the start of a session when it is completed, when it becomes impossible or when the character's motivations truly change in the story.

Desire

Desire represents what the character wants to achieve now. It should be fairly immediate and can come from the circumstances of the story, a relationship with another character or an opportunity that comes up during play. It does not need to be related to the Ambition, though it can be.

Examples of Desires:

  • convincing someone to reveal information;
  • gaining access to a restricted area;
  • impressing an important person;
  • recovering an item;
  • finding out who is following the group;
  • winning a negotiation;
  • humiliating a rival;
  • finding a way into a building.

A good Desire represents something the character truly wants and that influences their decisions during the session.

Fulfilling a Desire

Once per session, when the character acts decisively to fulfill their Desire, they recover 1 point of superficial Willpower damage, immediately, at the moment of the action.

Fulfilling the Desire ends it.

Changing the Desire

The Desire can only be set or changed at the start of a session. The player can keep the same Desire for several sessions, until it is fulfilled. Once fulfilled, the character has no Desire until the start of the next session, when they choose a new one.

Ambition and Desire in the Story

The Narrator can use Ambitions to create opportunities, enemies, allies and conflicts tied to the group's goals, and Desires to give direction to each session's immediate decisions. Incompatible Ambitions or Desires between characters also make for good conflicts. These traits do not determine how the character must act: they show what they consider important at that moment.

Ambition represents what the character intends to achieve over the course of the story.

Desire represents what they want to achieve now.

regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.title: Convictions and Pillars
regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.summary: A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray — for example, "Never abandon those who fight at my side". Unlike Ambition and Desire, a Conviction is not a goal: it is a line of conduct.
regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.text:
A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray — for example, "Never abandon those who fight at my side".
Unlike Ambition and Desire, a Conviction is not a goal: it is a line of conduct.
Convictions
Every character has 3 Convictions, chosen during character creation (see Identity).
Pillars
Each Conviction must be sustained by a Pillar: a concrete person, place or object in the story that embodies that Conviction — for example, a traveling companion or a father's diary.
The Pillar gives the Narrator something tangible to put at risk.
Turning to a Pillar
Once per session, in total, outside a Tactical Scene, the character can turn to one of their Pillars: talk with the person, visit the place or spend time with the object. The scene must be played out, even briefly, and show what the Pillar means to the character. At its end, 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage becomes superficial damage.
The Pillar must be present: a destroyed or lost Pillar cannot be sought out.
Fractures
Each Conviction withstands 2 Fractures. A Conviction can be:
Intact — no Fractures;
with 1 Fracture;
with 2 Fractures, which breaks it (see Broken Conviction).
Gaining a Fracture
A Conviction gains 1 Fracture when:
the character deliberately acts against it; or
its Pillar is harmed or corrupted.
On gaining a Fracture, the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage.
Repairing a Fracture
At the end of a session in which the character defended a Conviction that is not broken, or its Pillar, paying a real cost — such as risk, loss or sacrifice —, remove 1 Fracture from that Conviction. Repairing a Fracture turns 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage into superficial damage.
This can happen once per session for each Conviction. An intact Conviction has no Fracture to repair: defending it does not convert Willpower damage.
Broken Conviction
A Conviction breaks when:
it receives its second Fracture; or
its Pillar is destroyed or lost. In that case, the Conviction goes straight to 2 Fractures, and the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage for each Fracture gained this way.
While there are broken Convictions, every purchase made with XP costs 2 more XP for each broken Conviction, up to a maximum of 6 more XP.
Restoring a Broken Conviction
A broken Conviction is not repaired through Fractures. During the campaign, the character must actively seek that restoration in the story.
The player and the Narrator decide together whether the Conviction will be restored or replaced by a new Conviction, with its own Pillar.
Restored — including when the lost Pillar is recovered: the Conviction loses both Fractures, gets its Pillar back and up to 2 points of aggravated Willpower damage become superficial.
Replaced — the new Conviction starts intact, with no Fractures.
Benefit
Once per session, in total and not for each Conviction, when the character acts in defense of a Conviction or its Pillar, they can use Willpower without taking the superficial Willpower damage, whether to Reroll Dice or to Ignore Physical Penalties.

The benefit does not pay the Willpower costs of Capabilities. A broken Conviction does not grant this benefit.
Convictions in the Story
The Narrator can use Pillars to create dilemmas between the character's Convictions, their Ambition and their Desire — for example, when protecting a Pillar means giving up progress toward the Ambition.

regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.html:
A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray — for example, "Never abandon those who fight at my side".

Unlike Ambition and Desire, a Conviction is not a goal: it is a line of conduct.

Convictions

Every character has 3 Convictions, chosen during character creation (see Identity).

Pillars

Each Conviction must be sustained by a Pillar: a concrete person, place or object in the story that embodies that Conviction — for example, a traveling companion or a father's diary.

The Pillar gives the Narrator something tangible to put at risk.

Turning to a Pillar

Once per session, in total, outside a Tactical Scene, the character can turn to one of their Pillars: talk with the person, visit the place or spend time with the object. The scene must be played out, even briefly, and show what the Pillar means to the character. At its end, 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage becomes superficial damage.

The Pillar must be present: a destroyed or lost Pillar cannot be sought out.

Fractures

Each Conviction withstands 2 Fractures. A Conviction can be:

  • Intact — no Fractures;
  • with 1 Fracture;
  • with 2 Fractures, which breaks it (see Broken Conviction).

Gaining a Fracture

A Conviction gains 1 Fracture when:

  • the character deliberately acts against it; or
  • its Pillar is harmed or corrupted.

On gaining a Fracture, the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage.

Repairing a Fracture

At the end of a session in which the character defended a Conviction that is not broken, or its Pillar, paying a real cost — such as risk, loss or sacrifice —, remove 1 Fracture from that Conviction. Repairing a Fracture turns 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage into superficial damage.

This can happen once per session for each Conviction. An intact Conviction has no Fracture to repair: defending it does not convert Willpower damage.

Broken Conviction

A Conviction breaks when:

  • it receives its second Fracture; or
  • its Pillar is destroyed or lost. In that case, the Conviction goes straight to 2 Fractures, and the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage for each Fracture gained this way.

While there are broken Convictions, every purchase made with XP costs 2 more XP for each broken Conviction, up to a maximum of 6 more XP.

Restoring a Broken Conviction

A broken Conviction is not repaired through Fractures. During the campaign, the character must actively seek that restoration in the story.

The player and the Narrator decide together whether the Conviction will be restored or replaced by a new Conviction, with its own Pillar.

  • Restored — including when the lost Pillar is recovered: the Conviction loses both Fractures, gets its Pillar back and up to 2 points of aggravated Willpower damage become superficial.
  • Replaced — the new Conviction starts intact, with no Fractures.

Benefit

Once per session, in total and not for each Conviction, when the character acts in defense of a Conviction or its Pillar, they can use Willpower without taking the superficial Willpower damage, whether to Reroll Dice or to Ignore Physical Penalties.

This use is possible even with a full Willpower track.

The benefit does not pay the Willpower costs of Capabilities. A broken Conviction does not grant this benefit.

Convictions in the Story

The Narrator can use Pillars to create dilemmas between the character's Convictions, their Ambition and their Desire — for example, when protecting a Pillar means giving up progress toward the Ambition.

Convictions do not dictate how the character must act. The player always decides what to do; the Fractures record the consequences of that choice.

regras/personagens/progressao.title: Advancement
regras/personagens/progressao.summary: In Astra, characters have no global levels. They grow gradually by acquiring and improving abilities over the campaign, paid for with Experience Points (XP).
regras/personagens/progressao.text:
In Astra, characters have no global levels. They grow gradually by acquiring and improving abilities over the campaign, paid for with Experience Points (XP).
Experience Points
XP received is added to the character's available total. When XP is spent on an improvement, its cost is removed from that total. The character can save XP for as many sessions as they want.
Awarding XP
Each campaign sets its own pace of advancement, at the Narrator's discretion. The Narrator can, for example, award XP at the end of each session or only when missions are completed.
As a suggestion, each character receives:
2 XP at the end of each session
For a slower pace or a short session, the Narrator can award 1 XP. For a session that represents a major milestone of the campaign, 3 XP.
It is recommended to give every character in the group the same amount of XP, keeping them at the same pace of advancement.
Spending Experience
XP can be used to:
raise Attributes;
raise Skills;
acquire or raise Competencies;
acquire or develop abilities specific to a setting or module.
Raising a trait means buying its next level. Intermediate levels cannot be skipped. When a rule uses the term new level, use the value the trait will have after the purchase.
Attributes and Skills go up to 5. Each Competency goes up to the maximum Level of its progression.
When an Attribute increases, every derived value whose formula currently uses that Attribute, such as Health, Willpower, Load and Initiative, is recalculated immediately (see Derived Traits).
If a Capability replaced the Attribute of a formula, the value follows the replacement. For example, if the character's Health uses Cunning instead of Vigor, raising Cunning recalculates their Health, while raising Vigor does not change it.
Experience Costs
Improvement Cost 
Raise an Attribute new level × 5 XP 
Raise a Skill new level × 3 XP 
Acquire or raise a Competency new Total Competency Level × 3 XP (see Competencies) 
Master one more weapon 3 XP (see Mastering a Weapon) 
Other abilities set by the rule, setting or module 
While the character has broken Convictions, every purchase costs +2 XP for each broken Conviction (see Broken Conviction).
Examples
Raising an Attribute from 2 to 3 costs 15 XP.
Raising a Skill from 2 to 3 costs 9 XP.
A character with Total Competency Level 2 pays 9 XP to acquire one more Competency Level, whether in a Competency they already have or in a new one.
Character Development
Advancement through experience lets characters who went through the same adventures develop in different ways: one can focus their XP on a few abilities, while another spreads it across different Skills, Competencies and other options.

criacao-de-personagem/criacao-de-persona.title: Character Creation
criacao-de-personagem/criacao-de-persona.summary: Character Creation is the process of building a new character in Astra. The result is a sheet ready to play, with identity, Attributes, Skills, Competencies and starting equipment. The steps are done in order, but you…
criacao-de-personagem/criacao-de-persona.text:
Character Creation is the process of building a new character in Astra. The result is a sheet ready to play, with identity, Attributes, Skills, Competencies and starting equipment.
The steps are done in order, but you can go back and adjust earlier choices while the character's concept takes shape.
Subsections
Identity — Concept, Ambition, Desire, Convictions and Pillars.
Attributes and Skills — Attributes (fixed values) and Skills (profiles).
Derived Traits — Health, Willpower, Initiative and Maximum Load.
Competencies — 2 Competency Points.
Starting Equipment — what the character starts out carrying.
Finally, round out the character with a name, appearance and backstory. The sheet is ready to play; later adjustments, spending XP, follow the Advancement rules.

criacao-de-personagem/identidade.title: Identity
criacao-de-personagem/identidade.summary: Before and beyond the numbers, a character is defined by who they are: their concept and what drives them. This subsection gathers those choices.
criacao-de-personagem/identidade.text:
Before and beyond the numbers, a character is defined by who they are: their concept and what drives them. This subsection gathers those choices.
Concept
Define who the character is in a few words: origin, occupation, personality and what drives them. The concept guides the following choices — which Attributes to prioritize and which Competencies to develop.
Ambition and Desire
Choose 1 Ambition and 1 Desire (see Ambition and Desire).
Ambition is a long-term goal; Desire, something immediate.
Convictions and Pillars
Choose 3 Convictions and the Pillar that sustains each one (see Convictions and Pillars).
A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray; the Pillar, the person, place or object that embodies it.
Agree on the Pillars with the Narrator, because they become part of the story.

criacao-de-personagem/atributos-e-perici.title: Attributes and Skills
criacao-de-personagem/atributos-e-perici.summary: Beyond the concept, a character is defined numerically by their Attributes and Skills. This subsection covers the starting distribution of points between them.
criacao-de-personagem/atributos-e-perici.text:
Beyond the concept, a character is defined numerically by their Attributes and Skills. This subsection covers the starting distribution of points between them.
Attributes
Every character has the six core Attributes, with values from 1 to 5 (see Scale).
Distribute the values below among the six Attributes, choosing where each one goes:
One Attribute at 4 · two at 3 · two at 2 · one at 1
Skills
Skills range from 0 to 5 (see Scale). Each Skill has a linked Attribute, normally used to form its Dice Pool.
The core has 24 Skills. Start with all of them at 0 and choose one of the three profiles:
Generalist — one Skill at 3, six at 2 and six at 1.
Balanced — two at 3, four at 2 and six at 1.
Specialist — one at 4, two at 3, two at 2 and two at 1.
Skills that get no points stay at 0. Points can also go into a Specific Knowledge, and each Level in Scholarship gives an additional language.
Cap during creation
During creation, no Attribute or Skill goes above 4. The value 5 is only reached with XP.

criacao-de-personagem/caracteristicas-de.summary: Some of the character's values are not chosen directly: they are calculated from the Attributes. Trait Default formula. Health 3 + Vigor boxes (see Health). Willpower 3 + Determination boxes (see Willpower). Initiative…
criacao-de-personagem/caracteristicas-de.text:
Some of the character's values are not chosen directly: they are calculated from the Attributes.
Trait Default formula 
Health 3 + Vigor boxes (see Health) 
Willpower 3 + Determination boxes (see Willpower) 
Initiative Pool of Cunning + Determination, rolled at the start of the Scene (see Initiative) 
Maximum Load 5 + Strength (see Load) 
Replacements in formulas
Capabilities and other rules can replace an Attribute used in a derived trait. The replacement affects only the given formula, does not add the two Attributes together and does not change their other roles.
For example, if a Capability says Health uses Cunning instead of Vigor, its formula becomes:
Health = 3 + Cunning
This replacement does not make Cunning work as Vigor in tests, recovery or any other rule.
When the Attribute that currently makes up a derived trait increases, the value is recalculated immediately, and new Health or Willpower boxes start empty. Capabilities always take precedence over the default formulas.

criacao-de-personagem/competencias.text:
Besides Attributes and Skills, the character has Competencies that represent developed ways of acting and grant fixed progressions of Capabilities.
The character receives:
2 Competency Points
Each point raises a Competency by 1 Level and automatically grants that Level's content.
The points can be used to start with:
Level 2 in one Competency; or
Level 1 in two different Competencies.
The Levels acquired also set the character's Total Competency Level.
The points are spent during creation: they cannot be saved or converted into XP.
See the list of Competencies for the available options.

criacao-de-personagem/equipamento-inicia.summary: Every character starts with some equipment. What they carry at first is set by the setting being played. The setting can offer: a ready-made starting package; or. a budget in Value, for the player to buy from the…
criacao-de-personagem/equipamento-inicia.text:
Every character starts with some equipment. What they carry at first is set by the setting being played. The setting can offer:
a ready-made starting package; or
a budget in Value, for the player to buy from the catalog.
Without guidance from the setting, use a budget of 100 Value.
Every item has a Value, and the currency used varies by setting.
The core offers the Weapon Catalog, the Armor Catalog, the Shield Catalog, the Consumable Catalog and the Item Catalog. The setting can limit, replace or expand these options.
The character can carry items up to their Maximum Load; going beyond that leaves them Overloaded.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/cenas-taticas.title: Tactical Scenes
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/cenas-taticas.summary: Tactical Scenes in Astra represent conflicts in which position, timing, movement and the decisions made during the Scene directly matter to the outcome. Using a map is recommended, with characters and other Scene…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/cenas-taticas.text:
Tactical Scenes in Astra represent conflicts in which position, timing, movement and the decisions made during the Scene directly matter to the outcome.
Using a map is recommended, with characters and other Scene elements occupying specific positions in squares.
Without a map, combat is run narratively: the Narrator describes positions and distances and decides, from that description, which targets are within reach and which moves are possible.
During a Tactical Scene, time is organized into Rounds and Turns. The whole conflict is treated as a single Tactical Scene.
Narrative or tactical
Not every Scene needs to be resolved at the same level of detail.
In more narrative situations, the focus is on the characters' decisions, the consequences of their actions and the development of the Scene as a whole. In those moments, there is no need to track precisely elements such as position, acting order, distances, movement or the exact duration of each action.
When those elements start to matter directly to the conflict, the Scene can take on a more tactical structure.
In a Tactical Scene, the game uses more precise rules to represent what happens moment to moment. The participants' order is set by Initiative, time is divided into Rounds and Turns, positions and distances can be tracked on a map, and each character manages resources such as their Action and their Movement.
This shift does not have to happen only in combat. Chases, escapes, infiltrations under pressure, collapses, traps or any other situation in which order, timing and positioning matter can also use a tactical structure.
Likewise, not every conflict needs to be handled this way. A quick fight, a riskless crossing or an action whose exact position does not matter can still be resolved narratively, using tests and decisions without dividing the Scene into Turns.
The purpose of this distinction is to let Astra use precision when it really adds something to the Scene, without turning every situation into a rigid sequence of actions, moves and measurements.
Rounds, Turns and Initiative are in The Scene.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.title: The Scene
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.summary: A Scene is a unit of play, whether narrative or tactical. A Scene ends when the place, the moment or the situation changes enough for the Narrator to move on to another. Effects that last "until the end of the Scene"…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.text:
A Scene is a unit of play, whether narrative or tactical. A Scene ends when the place, the moment or the situation changes enough for the Narrator to move on to another. Effects that last "until the end of the Scene" end at that point.
A Tactical Scene is a Scene divided into Rounds and Turns. It starts when a conflict calls for a resolution structured in Turns and lasts until the conflict ends, whether by the defeat of one side, flight, surrender, a change in circumstances or any other outcome set by the narrative.
Within the Tactical Scene, time is divided into Rounds.
Rounds and Turns
A Round represents a full cycle of the Scene, in which every participant has the chance to act.
Within each Round, participants take their Turns in the order set by Initiative.
A Turn represents the moment when a character can act directly in the Scene.
After every participant has taken their Turn, a new Round begins, keeping the same Initiative order as long as no rule or circumstance says otherwise.
Initiative
Initiative sets the order in which participants take their Turns during the Scene.
At the start of the Scene, each participant rolls a Dice Pool made of Cunning and Determination and counts Successes as usual.
Cunning + Determination = Initiative Pool
Capabilities and other rules can replace one of the Initiative Attributes or set a different Pool. When a Capability does so, it takes precedence over the default formula.
Participants act from the highest number of Successes to the lowest.
Whoever joins the Scene after it starts rolls Initiative on arrival and takes their place in the order from then on.
Ties
When a player character and an NPC tie, the player character acts first.
When two or more player characters get the same number of Successes, they can decide among themselves the order in which they act.
If they cannot agree, the Narrator sets the order.
When two or more NPCs tie, the one with the highest Cunning acts first. If the tie remains, the Narrator sets the order.
Surprise
A participant who does not notice the threat when the Tactical Scene starts, as in an ambush, is surprised until their first Turn. While surprised, they are a target without a response. The Narrator decides who notices the threat and can call for a Cunning + Perception test against the Agility + Stealth of whoever is hiding.
The Turn
During their Turn, a character has:
Action + Movement
The Action and the Movement can be used in whatever order the player prefers.
A character can, for example, move before taking their Action or act first and move afterward, or even move, act and move again if they still have movement points left, as explained in Movement.
How these resources are used depends on the character's decisions and the circumstances of the Scene.
To know when to use the tactical structure, see Tactical Scenes.
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.html:
A Scene is a unit of play, whether narrative or tactical. A Scene ends when the place, the moment or the situation changes enough for the Narrator to move on to another. Effects that last "until the end of the Scene" end at that point.

A Tactical Scene is a Scene divided into Rounds and Turns. It starts when a conflict calls for a resolution structured in Turns and lasts until the conflict ends, whether by the defeat of one side, flight, surrender, a change in circumstances or any other outcome set by the narrative.

Within the Tactical Scene, time is divided into Rounds.

Rounds and Turns

A Round represents a full cycle of the Scene, in which every participant has the chance to act.

Within each Round, participants take their Turns in the order set by Initiative.

A Turn represents the moment when a character can act directly in the Scene.

After every participant has taken their Turn, a new Round begins, keeping the same Initiative order as long as no rule or circumstance says otherwise.

Initiative

Initiative sets the order in which participants take their Turns during the Scene.

At the start of the Scene, each participant rolls a Dice Pool made of Cunning and Determination and counts Successes as usual.

Cunning + Determination = Initiative Pool

Capabilities and other rules can replace one of the Initiative Attributes or set a different Pool. When a Capability does so, it takes precedence over the default formula.

Participants act from the highest number of Successes to the lowest.

Whoever joins the Scene after it starts rolls Initiative on arrival and takes their place in the order from then on.

Ties

When a player character and an NPC tie, the player character acts first.

When two or more player characters get the same number of Successes, they can decide among themselves the order in which they act.

If they cannot agree, the Narrator sets the order.

When two or more NPCs tie, the one with the highest Cunning acts first. If the tie remains, the Narrator sets the order.

Surprise

A participant who does not notice the threat when the Tactical Scene starts, as in an ambush, is surprised until their first Turn. While surprised, they are a target without a response. The Narrator decides who notices the threat and can call for a Cunning + Perception test against the Agility + Stealth of whoever is hiding.

The Turn

During their Turn, a character has:

Action + Movement

The Action and the Movement can be used in whatever order the player prefers.

A character can, for example, move before taking their Action or act first and move afterward, or even move, act and move again if they still have movement points left, as explained in Movement.

How these resources are used depends on the character's decisions and the circumstances of the Scene.

To know when to use the tactical structure, see Tactical Scenes.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acao.summary: An Action is what a character does on their Turn besides Movement: attacking, performing maneuvers, using objects, interacting with the environment or any other activity relevant to the situation. When an Action has its…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acao.text:
An Action is what a character does on their Turn besides Movement: attacking, performing maneuvers, using objects, interacting with the environment or any other activity relevant to the situation.
When an Action has its own rule, that rule sets how it is resolved. Confront, for example, starts an Attack against another character.
Basic Actions
Basic Actions are the most common ways to act in a Tactical Scene and have their own procedures. Whenever one of them represents what the character wants to do, use its rule, even if the activity is described another way.
Confront
Run
Wait
Switching Equipment
Maneuvers
Narrative Actions
When no Basic Action or other rule represents the character's intent, such as opening a door, pulling a lever or helping someone, the Action is narrative: the Narrator decides whether the activity fits in a single Action and whether it calls for a test.
An Action is a meaningful activity, not a single movement. Simple, continuous activities do not need to be split up: taking a potion from a bag and drinking it, for example, is a single Action.
Saying a few words, making a gesture or dropping an object does not take an Action.
Limits
This does not allow grouping any number of activities. The Narrator weighs the time available, the complexity of the activity and the circumstances of the Scene. Activities with separate goals, lengthy procedures or their own rules take separate Actions.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/confronta.summary: A Confront happens when a character uses their Action to attack another character during a Tactical Scene. When starting a Confront, the attacker builds a Dice Pool according to the kind of Attack used. Kind of Attack…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/confronta.text:
A Confront happens when a character uses their Action to attack another character during a Tactical Scene.
When starting a Confront, the attacker builds a Dice Pool according to the kind of Attack used.
Kind of Attack Default Pool 
Melee Agility + Fighting 
Shooting weapon Agility + Shooting 
Thrown weapon Strength + Throwing 
The weapon, a Capability or another rule can set a different Attribute or Pool. Capabilities always take precedence over other replacements.
The Heavy property replaces Agility with Strength without changing the Skill: a Heavy melee weapon uses Strength + Fighting, while a Heavy shooting weapon uses Strength + Shooting. It does not add Strength to the damage.
Two-Weapon Fighting
Every character can use one weapon in each hand by default. This lets them keep two weapons with different types and properties at hand, but by itself it grants no extra dice, damage or Attacks.
On each Confront, whether attacking or responding, the character chooses which of the two weapons to use:
the main weapon is the chosen weapon. It sets the Pool, the Damage, the Damage Type and the Mastery of the Confront;
the off-hand weapon is the one in the other hand. It has no effect on the Confront, unless a Capability, such as those of Ambidextrous, says otherwise.
Unarmed, Natural weapons and Shields do not count as an off-hand weapon, except a shield with Shield Bash.
Responding to the Confront
After the attacker declares the Confront, the target character must choose how to respond.
They can:
Accept the Confront
Defend
Dodge
The chosen response sets how the test is resolved and which consequences can follow:
Response Pool Target wins Tie Attacker wins 
Accept the Confront the target's Attack Pool Margin as superficial damage weapon Damage, superficial Margin + weapon Damage 
Defend Strength + Fighting + Protection no damage weapon Damage, superficial Margin + weapon Damage 
Dodge Agility + Acrobatics no damage and moves up to half base Movement weapon Damage, superficial Margin + weapon Damage 
Accept the Confront
When they Accept the Confront, the character does not merely try to avoid the Attack. They respond by striking back.
Both characters build their Dice Pools and make an opposed roll.
Whoever gets more Successes wins the Confront.
If the attacker wins, they deal damage equal to:
Margin of Successes + weapon Damage
If the one who accepted the Confront wins, the counterattack deals only:
Margin of Successes, as superficial damage
The weapon's Damage does not apply to the counterattack.
The Margin is the difference between the number of Successes the two participants got.
If both get the same number of Successes, it is a tie and the attacker wins, but deals only the weapon's Damage as superficial damage.
To Accept the Confront, you must be able to hit the attacker with the weapon used (see Reach and Confront Responses).
Defend
A character equipped with a Shield can choose to Defend. Some Capabilities allow Defending another way, such as Parry and Cover Ally.
In that case, they make a roll opposed to the Attack. The Dice Pool used is:
Strength + Fighting
The Shield's Protection is added to the Dice Pool.
If the defender gets more Successes than the attacker, the Attack is blocked and neither participant deals damage.
The tie and the attacker's win follow the response table.
Defending is not a counterattack. Even when they win the roll, the character only keeps the Attack from hitting them.
Dodge
A character can choose to Dodge to try to avoid the Attack entirely.
The Dice Pool used is:
Agility + Acrobatics
Capabilities and other rules can replace this Pool. Describing the Dodge differently does not allow freely using another Attribute or Skill. Medium and Heavy armor reduce this Pool (see Armor).
If the character gets more Successes than the attacker, they avoid the damage entirely and can immediately move up to:
half their base Movement
in a direction of their choice.
This move follows the usual Movement rules, such as Difficult Terrain and Special Movement, but does not trigger effects provoked by movement, such as abilities that punish or interfere with opponents' movement.
The tie and the attacker's win follow the response table.
A character who is unable to move cannot choose to Dodge.
Target without a Response
When the target cannot respond to the Confront, whether because they are surprised, unconscious, Incapacitated, Paralyzed or have no valid response, only the attacker rolls. The target's result always counts as 1 Success.
The Confront is resolved as usual with that value, including the tie rule. If the attacker gets no Successes, the Attack fails and no one takes damage.
Numerical Advantage
When several characters surround the same enemy, the numerical advantage opens gaps in their defense.
When starting a Confront against an enemy, the attacker gets +1 die for each ally they have beyond the enemy side in that fight:
Numerical Advantage Bonus = allies adjacent to the target - (the target + the target's allies adjacent to them)
The attacker counts themselves among the allies adjacent to the target. The bonus is never negative.
Situation Bonus for each attacker 
1 × 1 +0 
2 × 1 +1 
3 × 1 +2 
3 × 2 +1 
2 × 2 +0 
To count the sides:
Adjacent includes diagonals. A creature that takes up more than one square is adjacent to everything next to any square it occupies (see Size).
The attacker must also be adjacent to the target.
Incapacitated characters do not count for either side.
Player characters are always allies of each other. Each NPC belongs to a side, which can be hostile, neutral or allied with the group.
Numerical Advantage applies only to melee Attacks. When the surrounded enemy attacks, the characters who respond (Accepting the Confront, Defending or Dodging) do not get the bonus.
Attacking Beyond Range
A weapon's Range is the maximum distance, in squares, at which it hits its targets without penalty.
Ranged Attacks, including thrown weapons, can hit targets beyond the weapon's normal Range. For each band of squares the size of the weapon's Range beyond its normal Range, the attacker suffers -2 dice to their Dice Pool on the Attack.
A weapon with Range 6 hits targets up to 6 squares away normally. A target between 7 and 12 squares imposes -2 dice on the Attack; between 13 and 18 squares, -4 dice; and so on.
For thrown weapons, use the throwing Range instead of the weapon's Range (see Thrown).
If the loss reduces the Dice Pool below 1 die, the Attack cannot be made.
Reach and Confront Responses
The available response depends on the characters' positions and the equipment used.
Accept the Confront requires the character to be able to hit the attacker.
Melee weapons can start Confronts against characters using ranged weapons when they are within the necessary reach.
Likewise, characters using ranged weapons can start Confronts against melee characters, but those can only Accept the Confront if they have enough reach to hit the attacker.
Ranged weapon restriction: a character cannot Accept the Confront using a ranged weapon when the attacker uses a melee weapon, even if the attacker is within the weapon's Range. Against ranged Attacks, they can Accept as usual, as long as they can hit the attacker.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/manobras.title: Maneuvers
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/manobras.summary: Maneuvers are actions to gain an advantage in a Tactical Scene without dealing damage: changing another character's position or Condition, taking something out of their hands or setting up an Attack. Any character can…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/manobras.text:
Maneuvers are actions to gain an advantage in a Tactical Scene without dealing damage: changing another character's position or Condition, taking something out of their hands or setting up an Attack. Any character can try a Maneuver.
Performing a Maneuver
Performing a Maneuver takes an Action.
Maneuver Who starts it Target resists Effect 
Reposition Strength + Athletics Strength + Athletics moves the target 1 square 
Trip Strength + Athletics Strength + Athletics the target becomes Prone 
Grapple Strength + Athletics Strength + Athletics the target becomes Grappled 
Disarm Agility + Fighting Agility + Fighting the target drops an item they are holding 
Aim no roll — 1 stack of Aiming 
A Maneuver with a target is resolved through an opposed roll. If whoever starts it gets more Successes, the effect is applied. On a tie or a win for the target, nothing happens.
By default, a Maneuver with a target requires you to be adjacent to it. A Maneuver that uses another reach says so in its own description. The Maneuver (X) property allows performing the given Maneuver up to the weapon's Reach, but does not change its Pool or grant a bonus.
A target can accept the Maneuver; in that case, it works without a roll. A target who cannot resist follows the Target without a Response rule: their result counts as 1 Success.
No Maneuver deals damage, whatever the Margin. To hurt the opponent, use a Confront.
Reposition, Trip and Grapple only affect targets at most one Size category larger than you.
The Pools are fixed. Describing the Maneuver differently does not allow freely swapping its Attribute or Skill. Capabilities, equipment and other rules can set express replacements, and Capabilities always take precedence. Heavy changes only Attacks and, for that reason, does not change a Maneuver performed with the weapon.
Narrative Maneuvers
The Maneuvers described in this section do not represent every possible way to physically interfere with another character.
When a player tries something similar that is not covered by a specific Maneuver, the Narrator can treat it as a Narrative Maneuver.
In that case, the Narrator sets a Dice Pool, the way to resist and the consequences of a win, using the linked Attributes and the existing Maneuvers as a reference. If the same attempt becomes recurring, it should get a fixed formula. The narrative description does not allow simply swapping the Attribute of an existing Skill.
List of Maneuvers
Reposition
You try to move another character from their position. If you win, you move the target 1 square in the direction you choose. The move can represent a shove, a pull, steering the body or something similar.
Obstacles and Edges
Reposition can move a character toward obstacles, edges or other elements of the Scene.
If the move meets an obstacle that blocks movement, it stops. The collision by itself deals no additional damage.
If the chosen square takes the target off an edge, platform or similar position, the consequences of the fall or the environment are resolved as usual.
Trip
You try to put another character on the ground. If you win, the target gets the Prone Condition.
Grapple
You try to restrain another character with a free hand. If you win, the target gets the Grappled Condition.
Disarm
You try to make another character lose a piece of equipment they are holding, such as a weapon, a shield or another object. If you win, the target drops the chosen equipment in their own square.
Picking the equipment up from the ground takes the Switching Equipment Action, even with a free hand.
Aim
You use your Action to focus before a ranged Attack and get 1 stack of Aiming. Each stack gives +2 dice on the next ranged Attack, against any target.
Aiming does not spend your Movement, and you can move before Aiming. The stacks are lost if you move afterward, among other cases described in the Condition.
